summary: Gives a new Bidi rule for IDNA labels, to handle problems found when right-to-left scripts such as Arabic and Hebrew are used in internationalized domain names. It improves on shortcomings in the 2003 Bidi criterion. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Some languages are written from right to left. When these are mixed with left-to-right text in a web address, the order can get jumbled, so this sets rules to keep it sensible.

questions: why was the idna2003 bidi rule changed
subtitle: The six-part Bidi rule that decides which right-to-left domain labels are safe to display in IDNA2008.

tldr.problem: The 2003 IDNA Bidi criterion banned many valid words in right-to-left scripts, and for Dhivehi it banned every word, because labels there end in a combining mark.
tldr.mechanism: A new Bidi rule of six conditions checks the first character, the allowed character classes and the last character of each label, and keeps European and Arabic digits from mixing in one right-to-left label.
tldr.outcome: The rule is part of the revised IDNA protocol. Most labels allowed before are still allowed, so the operational impact is described as limited.

today: RFC 5893 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains part of the IDNA2008 document set alongside RFC 5891.

sections.title: Purpose and Applicability
sections.content:
RFC 5893 sets a rule for Internationalized Domain Name (IDN) labels in Unicode form (U-labels) that contain characters from scripts written right to left. It is part of the revised IDNA protocol defined in RFC 5891.

If a label satisfies the rule, and certain other conditions hold, there is only a minimal chance of it being displayed in a confusing way by the Unicode bidirectional display algorithm. The rule adds validity criteria on top of the other IDNA2008 documents, which list the permitted characters. It places no requirements on domain names that contain no characters from such scripts.
sections.plainLanguage: Some alphabets run right to left, and mixing them with left-to-right writing can scramble the order on screen. This rule picks which names are safe to show.

sections.title: The Problem with the 2003 Rule
sections.content:
Stringprep (RFC 3454), part of IDNA2003, required that if a string contains any RandALCat character (one with unambiguously right-to-left direction), such a character must be both the first and the last character of the string. The aim was to give every part of a displayed name a clear direction.

The side effect was that certain words in right-to-left languages became invalid labels. In the case of Dhivehi, every word of the language was forbidden. RFC 3454 also never stated the requirement it was meant to meet, so nobody could tell whether a relaxed rule would still meet it.

The new rule is quite different, but most reasonable labels allowed by RFC 3454 remain allowed. The main exceptions are labels that mix Arabic and European digits (AN and EN) inside a right-to-left label, and labels that use AN in a left-to-right label.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule said a right-to-left word had to start and end with a certain kind of letter. Many real words end with a small mark instead, so they were wrongly turned away.

sections.title: Bidi Classes and Terms
sections.content:
Every Unicode character has a Bidi property that controls how it behaves in the Unicode bidirectional algorithm. The RFC lists them, among them L (left to right), R (right to left, non-Arabic), AL (Arabic letters), EN (European number), AN (Arabic number), NSM (nonspacing mark such as a combining accent) and BN (boundary neutral).

An RTL label contains at least one character of type R, AL or AN. An LTR label is any label that is not an RTL label. A Bidi domain name contains at least one RTL label. Network order is the sequence as transmitted, and display order is the sequence as shown on screen.
sections.plainLanguage: Each letter is tagged with a direction, like arrows on a road. Words with right-pointing and left-pointing arrows need rules so traffic does not collide.

sections.title: The Bidi Rule
sections.content:
The rule has six conditions, and all of them must be satisfied. It applies to labels in Bidi domain names.

  • The first character must have Bidi property L, R or AL. R or AL makes it an RTL label, L makes it an LTR label.
  • In an RTL label, only R, AL, AN, EN, ES, CS, ET, ON, BN and NSM are allowed.
  • In an RTL label, the end must be R, AL, EN or AN, followed by zero or more NSM.
  • In an RTL label, if an EN is present no AN may be present, and the reverse.
  • In an LTR label, only L, EN, ES, CS, ET, ON, BN and NSM are allowed.
  • In an LTR label, the end must be L or EN, followed by zero or more NSM.

The RFC guarantees that a domain name made only of labels that satisfy the rule meets the requirements of the next section. Even LTR labels and pure ASCII labels have to be tested. A name made of LDH labels and compliant labels also meets them, as long as a label starting with an ASCII digit does not come after a right-to-left label. No guarantee is given for other combinations.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is a short checklist: start with a clear letter, use only allowed kinds of characters, end in a proper way, and do not mix two kinds of digits in one right-to-left word.

sections.title: The Requirements the Rule Meets
sections.content:
Unlike RFC 3454, this document states what the rule is for. There are two requirements, both assuming labels are displayed with the Unicode bidirectional algorithm.

  • Label Uniqueness: two labels displayed in the same paragraph should not look the same in character order unless they are also the same in network order, in both LTR and RTL paragraphs.
  • Character Grouping: when a string of labels is reordered for display, the characters of each label stay grouped between the delimiters, in both LTR and RTL paragraphs.

Stronger goals were considered and rejected as impossible within the Unicode algorithm. For example, the sequence of labels cannot always match network order: labels L1.R2.R3.L4 display as L1.R3.R2.L4 in an LTR context. The RFC also notes that testing found directional controls (LRE, RLE, RLO, LRO, PDF) do not change how a compliant name displays, though this is not stated as a requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two promises. Two different names should not end up looking identical, and each word should stay in one piece instead of its letters wandering into the next word.

sections.title: Dhivehi, Yiddish and Digits
sections.content:
Dhivehi, the official language of the Maldives, is written in the Thaana script, where every word ends with a combining mark. The word for computer, romanized as konpeetaru, ends with U+07AA THAANA UBUFILI, whose class is NSM and not R or AL, so IDNA2003 refuses to encode it.

Yiddish uses the Hebrew script, with combining points that also appear at the end of words. The YIVO acronym ends with U+05B8 HEBREW POINT QAMATS (NSM) and is rejected for the same reason. The RFC argues that barring pointed final characters is like saying a string of Latin letters cannot end with the letter p.

For numbers, the old rule meant a string with right-to-left characters could not end in a digit. The strings ALEF 5 and 5 ALEF display identically in an LTR context, so only one should be registrable, but banning both seemed unnecessary.
sections.plainLanguage: Some languages put little marks over or under the last letter of every word. The old rule treated those marks like a mistake and rejected the whole word.

sections.title: Limits and Compatibility
sections.content:
Some surprising displays remain. The most important case is a label ending in AL, AN or R followed by a label that begins with EN: the number appears to move into the right-to-left label. The working group did not require a fix, because ASCII names starting with digits are widely deployed, names are often built piecemeal, a DNAME could point an unsafe label at a safe one, and wildcards let labels resolve without the zone owner knowing. The RFC warns about it and leaves mitigation to application developers.

For backwards compatibility, an old program that checks input against RFC 3454 will refuse some newly allowed labels, or fall back to showing the A-label form, or display the final character inconsistently. The editors judged this less harmful than continuing to deny whole languages. Registries are advised to check for the leading-digit case, and it is generally best to disallow right-to-left strings in a zone whose parent label begins with a digit.

The rule depends on Unicode Bidi property values, which Unicode does not declare immutable, so a later Unicode version could change them. The RFC offers no solution for that.
sections.plainLanguage: Old programs that still use the old rule may refuse or oddly show the newly allowed names. The authors decided that is better than leaving whole languages out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mixed-direction text can display in surprising ways: copy and paste into a context with another direction can change how it looks, and adding a character in one place can move characters far from it. The RFC notes this is not unique to domain names.

The new rules allow some strings that IDNA2003 did not, and different interpretations between IDNA2003 and IDNA2008 implementations could pose a risk, though the RFC says it is hard to picture a specific one. A hash computed over an identifier would use network order and so would not be affected.
sections.plainLanguage: Text that goes both ways can look different after you copy it somewhere else, so people should be careful about what a name really says.
